text:
It's the same cause in both cases: air scatters blue light much more strongly than red light.

Sunlight looks white, but it's a mix of all colors. When it hits air molecules, the short wavelengths (blue) get bounced around far more than the long ones (red). During the day, that scattered blue light reaches your eyes from every part of the sky, so the whole sky looks blue.

At sunset, the sun is near the horizon, so its light has to cross much more air to reach you. Along that long path, most of the blue gets scattered out of the direct beam. What's left is mostly orange and red, so the sun and the sky near it take on those colors. Clouds light up for the same reason: they catch the leftover red light.

Two small footnotes:

- **Why not violet?** Violet scatters even more than blue, but the sun gives off less of it, the upper atmosphere absorbs some, and our eyes aren't very sensitive to it. Blue wins out.
- **Why some sunsets are more vivid:** Dust, smoke, and other particles in the air scatter even more of the blue, which is why sunsets can be especially red after wildfires or volcanic eruptions.
